question: To which north is VOR bearing information normally referenced?

options.text: Magnetic north at the aircraft
Magnetic north at the VOR
True north at the VOR
Grid north on the chart

explanation: A VOR is normally aligned so that its 000° radial points to magnetic north at the beacon itself. That is why variation at the station, not at the aircraft, is used when a VOR bearing is plotted.

question: Why can VOR be used equally well by day and by night?

options.text: It is VHF, so it has no sky wave and little static
It uses a lower frequency at night to avoid interference
It uses horizontal polarization, which the ionosphere ignores
Its ground monitor switches power up at night

explanation: VHF signals are not returned by the ionosphere and suffer little static, so VOR has none of the night effect that troubles ADF.

question: What frequency band does VOR use?

options.text: 962 to 1 213 MHz

explanation: VOR uses 108–117.95 MHz in the VHF band. The 108–112 MHz part is shared with the ILS localizer; 118–137 MHz is voice communication; 962–1 213 MHz is DME.

question: What type of fix does a VOR co-located with a DME provide?

options.text: A bearing and bearing (theta-theta) fix
A hyperbolic position fix
A range and bearing (rho-theta) fix
A range and range (rho-rho) fix

explanation: The VOR gives the radial (theta) and the DME the distance (rho), so one station gives an instantaneous position.

question: Which of these is a use of VOR?

options.text: Measuring the aircraft's height above terrain
Measuring distance to the station
Giving glide path guidance to the threshold
Defining the centre lines of airways

explanation: VORs mark the start, end and centre line of airway sections, serve as let-down aids and holding points, and give en route position lines.

question: How does a VOR receiver find the aircraft's bearing from the station?

options.text: By measuring the time for a pulse to travel from the station
By comparing the phase of two 30 Hz signals
By comparing the strength of two overlapping lobes
By finding the null of a rotating loop aerial

explanation: VOR works by phase comparison. A reference 30 Hz signal and a variable 30 Hz signal are compared; their phase difference equals the aircraft's magnetic bearing from the station.

question: In a conventional VOR, how is the reference 30 Hz signal transmitted?

options.text: Amplitude modulated, the same phase in all directions
Frequency modulated, varying in phase with bearing
Frequency modulated, the same phase in all directions
Amplitude modulated, varying in phase with bearing

explanation: The reference signal is a 30 Hz FM signal (carried on a subcarrier) whose phase is the same whatever the receiver's bearing. The directional signal is 30 Hz AM.

question: In a conventional VOR, how is the variable (directional) 30 Hz signal produced?

options.text: A pattern rotating 30 times a second gives 30 Hz AM
By a pattern rotating once per second, giving 1 Hz AM
By frequency modulating the carrier 30 times per second
By switching between two cardioids 120 times per second

explanation: A limaçon-shaped pattern rotates at 30 revolutions per second, so a receiver sees the signal strength rise and fall 30 times a second — a 30 Hz AM signal whose phase depends on bearing.

question: What shape is the rotating directional pattern of a conventional VOR?

options.text: A limaçon
A pencil beam
A figure-of-eight
A cardioid with no null

explanation: Combining a rotating figure-of-eight with the omnidirectional reference pattern produces a limaçon. Early VORs rotated the aerial mechanically; modern ones do it electronically.

question: Where are the reference and variable signals of a VOR in phase?

options.text: Due true north of the VOR
Due magnetic south of the VOR
Directly overhead the VOR
Due magnetic north of the VOR

explanation: The two 30 Hz signals are synchronised to be in phase on the 000° (magnetic) radial. Anywhere else the phase difference equals the magnetic bearing from the beacon.

question: Why are the two 30 Hz VOR signals put on by different types of modulation?

options.text: To allow the VOR to be used with ADF equipment
To double the range of the VOR
To stop them interacting and merging in the receiver
To give a 180° ambiguity that the receiver resolves

explanation: Using FM for one and AM for the other keeps the two 30 Hz signals separate, so the receiver can compare their phases.

question: An aircraft's VOR receiver measures a phase difference of 227°. On which radial is the aircraft?

options.text: The 047° radial
The 227° radial
The 317° radial
The 133° radial

explanation: The phase difference equals the magnetic bearing from the station, so the aircraft is on the 227° radial. Its QDM to the station is 047°.

question: Is VOR bearing information available while the station is transmitting its identification?

options.text: No, bearings are removed during the ident
Yes, bearing information is continuous
Only if the ident is sent in voice
Only on the 40 channels below 112 MHz

explanation: The bearing signals are transmitted continuously and are not interrupted by the Morse or voice identification.

question: What is a VOR radial?

options.text: A magnetic bearing from the VOR
A relative bearing of the VOR
A magnetic bearing to the VOR
A true bearing from the VOR

explanation: A radial is a magnetic bearing FROM the beacon — a QDR. The 090° radial runs east from the station.

question: An aircraft is on the 135° radial of a VOR. What is its QDM?
explanation: The QDM is the reciprocal of the radial: 135° + 180° = 315°. Flying 315°M (in still air) leads to the station.

question: An aircraft is on the 240° radial. Variation at the VOR is 10°W and at the aircraft 8°W. What true bearing from the VOR should be plotted?
explanation: Radials are referenced to magnetic north at the VOR, so the VOR's variation is used: true = magnetic − west variation = 240° − 10° = 230°. Using the aircraft's variation (232°) is the classic mistake.

question: How many VOR channels are available in total?
explanation: There are 40 channels between 108 and 112 MHz (shared with ILS) and 120 channels between 112 and 117.95 MHz, giving 160.

question: Between 108 and 112 MHz, which frequencies are used by VORs?

options.text: Odd first decimals, and odd decimals plus 0.05
Only whole and half megahertz
Every 0.05 MHz without exception
Even first decimals, and even decimals plus 0.05

explanation: In 108–112 MHz the ILS localizers take odd decimals (108.1, 108.15, 108.3…) and VORs take even ones (108.0, 108.05, 108.2, 108.25…).

question: Which frequency could be a VOR rather than an ILS localizer?
explanation: Below 112 MHz VORs use even first decimals (with or without the extra 0.05). 108.45 has an even first decimal (4); 108.10, 109.35 and 110.70 have odd first decimals and belong to localizers.

question: What is the channel spacing of VORs between 112 and 117.95 MHz?

options.text: 0.1 MHz
0.2 MHz
0.05 MHz

explanation: Above 112 MHz the band is VOR only, with a channel every 50 kHz — 120 channels.

question: What is the emission designator of VOR?

options.text: P0N
A3E
A9W
A8W

explanation: A9W: amplitude modulated double sideband (A), composite system (9), combination of telemetry, telephony and telegraphy (W).

question: How do UK VORs normally identify themselves?

options.text: A continuous tone with no Morse
Three-letter Morse at least every 10 seconds
Voice only, every minute
Two-letter Morse every 30 seconds

explanation: The ident is 3-letter Morse, about 7 groups per minute and at least every 10 seconds. A voice ident may follow, and the voice channel can carry ATIS at the same time as the bearings.

question: How does a test VOR (VOT) identify itself?

options.text: A continuous tone or a series of dots
Three-letter Morse every 10 seconds
A voice message giving its frequency
The letters TST in Morse

explanation: A VOT sends a continuous tone or a series of dots. A normal VOR sending TST is on test and must not be used.

question: How is ATIS sometimes provided through a VOR?

options.text: By interrupting the ident every 30 seconds
By replacing the bearing signal with speech
On the DME frequency paired with the VOR
On the VOR's voice channel, alongside the bearing information

explanation: The voice channel can carry ATIS by amplitude modulation at the same time as the bearing signals.

question: When will a VOR's automatic monitor remove the ident and navigation signals (or switch off the beacon)?

options.text: If the bearing changes by more than 5°
If the bearing changes by more than 1°
If the signal strength falls by more than 5%
If the ident fails for more than 1 minute

explanation: The monitor acts on a bearing change over 1°, a fall of more than 15% in signal strength (either 30 Hz modulation or the carrier), or failure of the monitor itself.

question: What reduction in signal strength triggers a VOR's monitor?

options.text: More than 15%
More than 25%
More than 5%
More than 50%

explanation: A reduction greater than 15% in either 30 Hz modulation, or the RF carrier, causes the monitor to warn and remove the signals.

question: What should a pilot assume if a VOR's bearings are present but no identification is heard?

options.text: It is serviceable; the ident is optional
It is serviceable but out of its DOC
It is a test VOR for checking equipment
It may be changing transmitters; do not use it

explanation: During a changeover to the standby transmitter no ident is sent and the bearings may be wrong until it stabilises. Never use a VOR without its ident.

question: A VOR is identifying "TST". What does this mean?

options.text: It is a test VOR for checking aircraft receivers
It is a broadcast VOR transmitting weather
It is on test; its bearings must not be used
It is a terminal VOR with reduced power

explanation: TST means the beacon is undergoing testing or maintenance. Its information should not be used for navigation.

question: What is a TVOR?

options.text: A low-power terminal VOR at major airfields
A VOR broadcasting weather between idents
A VOR co-located with TACAN
A VOR used only to test aircraft receivers

explanation: A terminal VOR transmits at low power (about 50 W) and serves the airfield area. A VORTAC is VOR with TACAN; a VOT is for testing; a BVOR broadcasts weather.

question: What is the main advantage of a Doppler VOR (DVOR)?

options.text: It gives distance as well as bearing
It works on a lower frequency band
It needs a special airborne receiver
It is much less sensitive to site error

explanation: DVOR is a second-generation VOR. It uses the same frequencies and airborne receivers, but its transmissions are far less affected by site error, so its bearings are more accurate.

question: In a Doppler VOR, how are the reference and variable signals modulated?

options.text: Both AM
Reference FM, variable AM
Reference AM, variable FM
Both FM

explanation: A DVOR reverses the conventional VOR's modulation: reference AM, variable FM.

question: Why does the simulated rotation of a Doppler VOR run anti-clockwise?

options.text: So that it rotates against the earth's rotation
So standard receivers still read the correct radial
So that it can be told apart from a conventional VOR
So that it gives twice the accuracy of a conventional VOR

explanation: Swapping AM and FM would reverse the phase relationship; rotating the pattern anti-clockwise restores it, so the same receiver works with CVOR and DVOR.

question: What is a VOT used for?

options.text: Checking the VOR receiver before IFR flight
Broadcasting ATIS between identifications
Navigating on a published approach procedure
Providing a back-up to the ILS glide path

explanation: A VOT radiates a single 360° radial in all directions. With the station not to be used for navigation, it lets pilots check receiver accuracy on the ground.

question: During a VOT check, what error means the aircraft's VOR equipment needs servicing?

options.text: More than ±10°
More than ±1°
More than ±4°
More than ±2°

explanation: A reading more than 4° from 360° (FROM) or 180° (TO) means the receiver needs attention.

question: What is a BVOR?

options.text: A VOR co-located with a TACAN
A VOR broadcasting weather and airfield information between idents
A VOR used only for testing receivers
A back-up VOR used when the main one fails

explanation: A broadcast VOR carries weather and airfield information between beacon identifications.

question: What is a VORTAC?

options.text: A VOR with a test function
A VOR used for terminal approaches
A Doppler VOR with a DME
A co-located VOR and TACAN

explanation: VORTAC combines a VOR with a military TACAN; civil aircraft use its DME element for range.

question: What range does an en route VOR with a 200 W transmitter typically have?

options.text: About 200 NM
About 500 NM
About 50 NM
About 25 NM

explanation: A 200 W en route VOR has a range of about 200 NM, subject to line of sight. A terminal VOR typically transmits only 50 W.

question: An aircraft at FL 160 is approaching a VOR whose aerial is at 900 ft. What is the maximum theoretical reception range?

options.text: About 160 NM
About 192 NM
About 1 920 NM
About 156 NM

question: What is VOR scalloping?

options.text: The cone of no signal directly over the station
Interference from a distant VOR transmitting on the same frequency
Errors caused by sky waves at night
Bends in a radial caused by reflections

explanation: Reflections from terrain and structures make the received radial bend, so the CDI needle drifts or swings from side to side. Known errors are published, e.g. "errors up to 5.5° in sector 315°–345° to 40 NM".

question: Why would co-frequency VORs ideally be separated by twice their line-of-sight range?

options.text: So that their radials never cross
So that the DME can tell them apart
So that an aircraft cannot receive both at once
So that their cones of silence never overlap

explanation: An aircraft at height can receive each beacon out to its line-of-sight range, so two beacons on the same frequency must be at least twice that far apart to avoid interference. With extra margins this becomes about 500 NM for planning.

question: For an aircraft at 25 000 ft and VORs at sea level, what minimum co-frequency separation would avoid interference?

options.text: About 250 NM
About 195 NM
About 389 NM
About 500 NM

explanation: Range = 1.23 × √25 000 ≈ 194.5 NM, and twice that is about 389 NM. Planning adds roughly 100 NM more, giving about 500 NM.

question: A VOR has a DOC of 80/30. What does this mean?

options.text: No co-frequency interference within 30 NM up to 8 000 ft
Accurate bearings within 80 NM above 3 000 ft only
Usable range 80 NM by day and 30 NM by night
No co-frequency interference within 80 NM up to 30 000 ft

explanation: DOC is range/altitude: within 80 NM and up to 30 000 ft the aircraft should not suffer co-frequency interference. It can vary by sector and is valid day and night.

question: Under what conditions may co-frequency interference occur within a VOR's DOC?

options.text: Thunderstorm static
Super-refraction
Sub-refraction
Heavy rain

explanation: Super-refraction bends VHF waves further than normal, so a distant VOR on the same frequency may be received inside the protected coverage.

question: To what accuracy is a VOR's ground site error monitored?
explanation: Site error from terrain, buildings, trees and even long grass near the transmitter is monitored to ±1°.

question: What is the maximum airborne equipment error permitted for VOR?
explanation: Converting the measured phase difference into a bearing introduces up to ±3° in the aircraft equipment.

question: What total VOR bearing error is usually assumed?
explanation: Site, propagation and airborne errors are aggregated to about ±5°. Pilotage error must be added, especially near the station where radials converge.

question: Why does flying accurately on a radial become harder close to a VOR?

options.text: Radials converge, so a degree is less distance
The VOR signal weakens close to the station because of the cone
Scalloping is always worst close to the station
The aircraft is inside the station's DOC

explanation: 1° of radial is about 1 NM wide at 60 NM but only about 0.1 NM at 6 NM, so the needle becomes very sensitive close in.

question: What happens to the VOR indications as the aircraft passes through the cone of ambiguity overhead?

options.text: The VOR indicates the 360° radial until the aircraft is clear of the cone
Needle swings, OFF may flicker, TO/FROM changes
The needle freezes and the last radial is held
The indications are unaffected; only DME is lost

explanation: There is no planned radiation directly above the beacon, so the indications become unreliable until the aircraft has passed through and readings settle.

question: Up to what minimum elevation angle must VOR coverage extend?
explanation: VOR must provide usable signals up to at least 40° above the horizon. Modern beacons usually manage 60–80°.

question: Where is the VOR aerial usually fitted on a high-speed aircraft?

options.text: A loop aerial under the fuselage
A parabolic dish in the nose
A whip aerial on top of the cockpit roof, ahead of the wing
Blade or flush aerials on the fin

explanation: Slow aircraft use a whip aerial on the fuselage; fast aircraft use blade or flush-mounted aerials on each side of the fin.

question: On a 5-dot VOR CDI, how many degrees does each dot represent?
explanation: On a 5-dot scale (the circle counts as the first dot) each dot is 2° and full-scale deflection is 10°.

question: What does full-scale deflection of a VOR CDI represent?

options.text: 5° or more off the selected radial
10° or more off the selected radial
20° or more off the selected radial
2.5° or more off the selected radial

explanation: Full deflection on a VOR display always represents 10° or more. Whether the scale has 5 dots (2° each) or 2 dots (5° each), the total is 10°.

question: A 5-dot CDI shows the bar 3 dots left of centre. How far is the aircraft from the selected course?
explanation: Each dot is 2°, so 3 dots = 6°.

question: On a 2-dot VOR display, how many degrees does each dot represent?
explanation: Full scale is still 10°, spread over 2 dots, so each dot is 5°.

question: Does the aircraft's heading affect the indication on a basic VOR CDI?

options.text: Yes; but only when inbound to the station
Yes; the bar always shows the turn needed
No; but the TO/FROM flag depends on heading
No; it depends only on position and the course set

explanation: The CDI shows the angle between the selected course and the radial the aircraft is on, and the TO/FROM is decided the same way. Heading plays no part.

question: A pilot flying outbound from a VOR has selected the inbound course, so the CDI shows TO. What is the problem?

options.text: The CDI will show the correct sense but the wrong radial
None; TO or FROM makes no difference to the sense
The CDI sense is reversed: a fly-left needs a right turn
The CDI will show OFF throughout the flight

explanation: To keep the deviation bar sensing correctly, select inbound tracks with TO showing and outbound tracks with FROM showing, with heading roughly the same as the selected course.

question: An aircraft is on the 090° radial and the pilot sets 090° on the OBS. What will the CDI show?

options.text: Needle full left with TO
Needle centred with OFF
Needle centred with TO
Needle centred with FROM

explanation: The aircraft is on the selected radial, so the needle is central. The course is within 90° of the radial the aircraft is on, so FROM is shown.

question: An aircraft is on the 090° radial and the pilot sets 270° on the OBS. What will the CDI show?

options.text: Needle centred with FROM
Needle centred with TO
Needle full left with TO
Needle full right with FROM

explanation: 270° is the QDM to the station from the 090° radial, so the aircraft is on the selected line, inbound: needle central, TO.

question: The OBS is set to 360°. The aircraft is on the 090° radial. What TO/FROM indication will be shown?

options.text: TO, with the needle centred
FROM
Neither; it is ambiguous or OFF
TO

explanation: 090° is 90° from the selected 360°, on the boundary between the TO and FROM sectors, so the indication is ambiguous (the sectors are about 20° wide in practice).

question: When a combined VOR/ILS indicator is used for VOR, what does the glide path needle show?

options.text: It is inoperative, centred and flagged OFF
It shows the aircraft's distance from the VOR
It shows the TO/FROM information
It shows the selected course error

explanation: The glide path pointer has no meaning on VOR, so it is centred and flagged. On ILS, the OBS has no effect and the TO/FROM is meaningless.

question: Which conditions bring up the OFF flag on a VOR indicator?

options.text: Being on a radial outside the DOC by day
Faulty signals, out of range, or inadequate power
Flying faster than 250 kt near the station
Being exactly on the selected radial

explanation: The OFF flag shows that the indication cannot be trusted: a faulty VOR transmission, being out of range, or an inadequate airborne power supply.

question: An aircraft is on the 200° radial with 020° set on the OBS. What does the CDI show?

options.text: Needle centred, TO
OFF flag only
Needle centred, FROM
Needle full-scale, TO

explanation: 020° is the QDM from the 200° radial, so the aircraft is on the selected line and the course leads to the station: centred, TO.

question: An aircraft is on the 095° radial with 090° set on the OBS. What does the CDI show?

options.text: Full-scale deviation, FROM
5° deviation (2.5 dots), TO
Centred, FROM
5° deviation (2.5 dots), FROM

explanation: The aircraft is 5° from the selected radial; at 2° per dot that is 2.5 dots. The course is within 90° of the aircraft's radial, so FROM.

question: With an RMI tuned to a VOR, what does the tail of the needle show?

options.text: The QDM to the VOR
The aircraft's magnetic heading
The radial the aircraft is on
The relative bearing of the VOR

explanation: The needle head shows the QDM to the station and the tail shows its reciprocal — the radial (QDR).

question: Before VOR information is shown on an RMI, what is done to it?

options.text: The aircraft's heading is added to give a true bearing
Heading is subtracted to give a relative bearing
Nothing; the RMI uses the raw phase difference
The variation is applied to give a true bearing

explanation: A differential synchro subtracts the magnetic heading from the VOR QDM to drive the needle. The compass card then adds the heading back, so the needle head reads the QDM.

question: An aircraft heading 040°M measures a VOR phase difference of 270°. Where will the RMI needle point?

options.text: 270° on the card, 230° right of the nose
090° on the card, 050° left of the nose
090° on the card, 050° right of the nose
310° on the card, 270° right of the nose

explanation: Phase difference 270° = 270° radial, so QDM = 090°. Relative bearing = 090° − 040° = 050°, and the needle points to 090° on the card.

question: If an RMI's heading input is in error, what happens to the VOR radial shown on it?

options.text: The RMI shows OFF until the heading is corrected
The radial is wrong by the amount of the heading error
Both radial and relative bearing are correct
Radial correct; relative bearing wrong

explanation: The VOR measures the radial independently of heading. A heading error shifts the card and needle together, so the needle still reads the right radial against the card, while the relative position to the nose is wrong.

question: Which is an advantage of an RMI over a CDI?

options.text: Two bearings and heading on one instrument
It needs no magnetic heading input
It is lighter and cheaper than a CDI
It shows the selected course error in dots

explanation: The RMI shows QDM, radial and heading together, gives a plan view useful in holds, shows rate of crossing radials, and a two-needle RMI shows two beacons at once (VOR or ADF). It is heavier, bulkier and more expensive than a CDI.

question: Which is a disadvantage of the RMI compared with a CDI?

options.text: It cannot show ADF bearings
It reverses sense when flying outbound
It shows only relative bearings
It is heavier, bulkier and more expensive

explanation: The RMI needs a remote-reading compass and its own power supplies, making it heavier, larger and costlier. In larger aircraft its advantages outweigh this.

question: Which navaids can be shown on a two-needle RMI?

options.text: VOR only
ADF only
Both VOR and ADF
ILS and DME

explanation: RMI needles can be switched to VOR or ADF, so two beacons — of either type — can be displayed together.

question: How does an HSI differ from a basic CDI for VOR navigation?

options.text: It needs no course to be selected by the pilot
It shows course and deviation on a heading card
It ignores the TO/FROM information entirely on all approaches
It shows only the QDM to the station

explanation: An HSI combines heading with course deviation: the selected course arrow rotates with the heading card, giving a plan view of the aircraft relative to the course.
